newsitem.title: DUBAI: U.S. forces in Gulf on heightened security alert.
newsitem.headline: U.S. forces in Gulf on heightened security alert.

text.p: U.S. military forces in the Gulf on Monday stepped up to a higher state of alert against attack by radicals, a U.S. Navy spokesman said.

Shore leave for the 12,000 U.S. sailors in the Gulf was restricted and clubs, bars and restaurants on the island state of Bahrain, headquarters of the U.S. Fifth Fleet, were placed off limits until further notice.
The U.S. embassy in the Bahraini capital Manama issued a security alert on its hotline recommending that U.S. civilians also avoid those places.
"Both the embassy and U.S. military continue to receive information about possible terrorist threats to U.S. military in the region, including Bahrain," said the spokesman.

"As such U.S. naval forces ashore have enhanced security posture. This is done since we continually evaluate security measures based on a regional threat. We adapt and adjust our measures as necessary."
A Gulf security source said the alert was designed to prevent large groups of Americans from gathering in open areas but there was no thought of sending U.S. families home.
A Western official said there had been a series of reports of possible terrorist threats to U.S. military forces in the region, including Bahrain.
U.S. naval forces in the Gulf comprise the aircraft carrier Theodore Roosevelt, cruisers, destroyers, submarines, logistics ships and pre-positioning equipment ships.

Osama bin Laden, branded by the U.S. State Department as one of the world's most significant sponsors of Islamic radical activities, has threatened to wage jihad (holy war or struggle) on Americans in the region -- in particular Saudi Arabia, homeland of Islam.

In an interview with Britain's Independent newspaper from his redoubt in the mountains of eastern Afghanistan last month, bin Laden warned Americans of a renewed onslaught against their forces in Saudi Arabia and said he had secured the support of thousands of Pakistanis for his campaign.
Officials in Washington have called him a prime suspect in two bombings in Saudi Arabia which killed 24 Americans and two Indians and injured more than 400 others in 1995 and 1996.
The U.S. embassies in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia routinely caution Americans about the need for vigilance.

The latest message from the embassy in Riyadh noted with deep concern an interview on British television in February "with well-known terrorist Osama bin Laden in which he not only threatened again the U.S. military in Saudi Arabia but also called for expulsion of American civilians".
